content:
# Building a Portfolio: Netlify, Docker & Modern Deployment

## Why This Stack?

Building a portfolio that showcases your work requires more than just a pretty website. You need:

- **Local development environment** that mirrors production
- **Easy deployment** without SSH or complex CI/CD
- **Fast iteration** on design and content
- **Scalability** as your portfolio grows

Netlify + Docker gives you all of this.

## Architecture

1. **Docker** for local dev and reproducible builds
2. **Netlify** for hosting and deployments
3. **GitHub** for version control and automation

## Getting Started

Create a Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "run", "dev"]
```

## Local Development

```bash
docker build -t portfolio .
docker run -p 3000:3000 portfolio
```

Visit `localhost:3000` to see your site.

## Deploy to Netlify

1. Push to GitHub
2. Connect repo to Netlify
3. Set build command: `npm run build`
4. Set publish directory: `out` or `dist`
5. Deploy

Netlify handles the rest — SSL, CDN, continuous deployment.

## Example: nitsuah.io

The portfolio at https://nitsuah.io uses this exact setup. See the live example.

title: Building a Small Project: Ollama + Neon + Next.js
content:
# Building a Small Project: Ollama + Neon + Next.js

## The Stack

- **Ollama** — Local LLM inference (no API keys)
- **Neon** — Serverless PostgreSQL
- **Next.js** — Full-stack React framework

## Why This Combo?

- **Ollama** runs locally → no OpenAI costs
- **Neon** free tier → PostgreSQL without ops
- **Next.js** API routes → backend without separate server

## Setup

### 1. Install Ollama

```bash
wget https://ollama.ai/download
./ollama serve
```

### 2. Pull a Model

```bash
ollama pull mistral  # or llama2, neural-chat
```

### 3. Create Neon Database

Sign up at neon.tech, create a project, grab the connection string.

### 4. Next.js API Route

```typescript
// pages/api/generate.ts
export default async function handler(req, res) {
  const { prompt } = req.body;
  
  const response = await fetch('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ model: 'mistral', prompt }),
  });
  
  res.status(200).json(await response.json());
}
```

## Database with Neon

```typescript
import { Pool } from 'pg';

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

export async function saveResult(prompt, result) {
  await pool.query(
    'INSERT INTO results (prompt, result) VALUES ($1, $2)',
    [prompt, result]
  );
}
```

## Example: vhsbox

See https://vhsbox.netlify.app for a live example of this pattern.

## Deployment

Deploy to Netlify Functions or Vercel. Ollama stays local; API routes call it.

This pattern ships fast without the ops overhead.

author: Austin H.
title: Building & Deploying a Chrome Extension with CI/CD
content:
# Building & Deploying a Chrome Extension with CI/CD

## The Challenge

Chrome extensions are great for automation, but:

- Manual updates are tedious
- Testing across versions is hard
- Deployment to the store requires manual steps
- Parsing and AI features add complexity

## The Solution: Full CI/CD

1. **Code** → push to GitHub
2. **Test** → run linting, unit tests, E2E in CI
3. **Build** → bundle extension
4. **Deploy** → push to Chrome Web Store automatically
5. **Monitor** → track updates and errors

## Project Structure

```
auto-apply-plugin/
├── src/
│   ├── content.ts      # Content script
│   ├── background.ts   # Service worker
│   └── popup.tsx       # UI
├── .github/workflows/
│   └── deploy.yml      # CI/CD pipeline
├── manifest.json
└── package.json
```

## GitHub Actions Workflow

```yaml
name: Build & Deploy
on: [push]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run test
      - run: npm run build
      - name: Upload to Chrome Web Store
        run: npm run deploy
        env:
          CHROME_EXTENSION_ID: ${{ secrets.CHROME_EXTENSION_ID }}
          CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN }}
```

## API & Parsing

```typescript
// background.ts
chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener(async (msg) => {
  if (msg.action === 'parse') {
    const result = await fetch('/api/parse', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify({ text: msg.text }),
    }).then(r => r.json());
    
    return result;
  }
});
```

## AI Integration

Use Ollama or OpenAI API for parsing:

```typescript
const response = await fetch('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({
    model: 'mistral',
    prompt: `Extract job details from: ${jobPosting}`,
  }),
});
```

## Example: auto-apply-plugin

See the live extension at https://github.com/nitsuah/auto-apply-plugin — fully automated CI/CD with AI-powered parsing.

## Takeaway

Chrome extensions don't have to be manual anymore. Full CI/CD + API integration + AI = shipping fast.

author: Austin H.
title: Building a GitHub Organization from Scratch
content:
# Building a GitHub Organization from Scratch

## Why Organization Structure Matters

As your projects grow, a flat repository list becomes unmanageable. GitHub Organizations let you:

- **Organize** repositories by team or product
- **Manage** permissions at scale with teams
- **Automate** workflows with GitHub Actions
- **Enforce** branch protection and code review policies

## Setting Up Your Organization

### Step 1: Create the Organization

1. Go to https://github.com/settings/organizations
2. Click "New organization"
3. Choose a plan (free tier is fine to start)
4. Set organization name, email, and description

### Step 2: Create Teams

Teams map to your internal structure:

```
Maintainers
├── Platform
├── AI/ML
└── DevOps

Contributors
├── Frontend
├── Backend
└── QA
```

Add team members and set permissions:

```bash
# Teams can have:
# - pull (read-only)
# - triage (read + label/close)
# - push (read + write)
# - maintain (write + settings)
# - admin (full access)
```

### Step 3: Repository Structure

Organize repos by function:

```
Platform Repos
├── core-api           (private, team: platform)
├── worker-service     (private, team: platform)
└── shared-types       (public, team: platform)

AI/ML Repos
├── model-training     (private, team: ai-ml)
├── inference-service  (private, team: ai-ml)
└── datasets           (private, team: ai-ml)

DevOps Repos
├── infrastructure     (private, team: devops)
├── deployment-tools   (public, team: devops)
└── monitoring         (private, team: devops)
```

### Step 4: Branch Protection

Protect main branches:

```yaml
# Settings > Branches > Protect main
- Require pull request reviews (2+)
- Require status checks to pass
- Require branches to be up to date
- Include administrators
- Restrict who can push
```

## Example: nitsuah GitHub Organization

The nitsuah org at https://github.com/nitsuah uses this structure across 15+ repositories.

## Best Practices

1. **One repo per service** — easier to scale, deploy independently
2. **Shared ownership** — multiple teams can contribute
3. **Consistent naming** — use prefixes: `core-`, `worker-`, `infra-`
4. **Clear permissions** — don't over-grant access
5. **Document team roles** — in README.md at org level

## Scaling Over Time

As teams grow:

- Add more granular teams
- Use GitHub Projects for cross-team planning
- Enforce code owners in CODEOWNERS file
- Automate team assignment with Actions

```bash
# CODEOWNERS file
/platform/*        @nitsuah/platform
/ai-ml/*           @nitsuah/ai-ml
/devops/*          @nitsuah/devops
```

This ensures reviews go to the right team automatically.

excerpt: Put safety rails around AI-generated code
author: Austin H.
title: Building Guardrails Around AI: Introducing Vigil
content:
# Building Guardrails Around AI: Introducing Vigil

## The Problem

AI-generated code is amazing but risky:

- ❌ Security vulnerabilities (SQL injection, hardcoded secrets)
- ❌ Performance issues (N+1 queries, memory leaks)
- ❌ Type errors (runtime crashes)
- ❌ Dead code (unused imports, variables)
- ❌ Inconsistent style (linting failures)

## The Solution: Vigil

**Vigil** is a GitHub Actions workflow that runs automated checks on AI-generated PRs before merge:

```yaml
name: Vigil - AI Code Guardrails
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  guardrails:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Run security scan
        run: npm run scan:security
      - name: Check types
        run: npm run typecheck
      - name: Lint code
        run: npm run lint
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm run test
```

## Features

### 1. Security Scanning

Detect dangerous patterns:

```typescript
// BAD: Hardcoded secret
const API_KEY = 'sk-1234567890';

// BAD: SQL injection
db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${userId}`);

// GOOD: Use environment variables
const API_KEY = process.env.API_KEY;

// GOOD: Use parameterized queries
db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [userId]);
```

### 2. Type Checking

Catch type errors before runtime:

```typescript
// TypeScript catches this
function add(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

add('5', '10'); // ❌ Error: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'
```

### 3. Linting

Enforce consistent style:

```bash
npm run lint --fix
```

### 4. Test Coverage

Ensure critical paths are tested:

```bash
npm run test -- --coverage
# Coverage must be > 80% for core modules
```

## Integration with AI

Use Vigil with Copilot or Claude:

```markdown
# Prompt for AI

Generate a function to fetch user data that passes:
- TypeScript type checking
- ESLint rules (no unused vars)
- Security scan (no hardcoded secrets)
- Test coverage > 80%

Here are the guardrails...
```

## Example: auto-apply-plugin

The auto-apply-plugin repository uses Vigil to guard against:
- XSS attacks in DOM manipulation
- Scope pollution in content scripts
- Memory leaks in event listeners

## Getting Started

1. Copy `.github/workflows/vigil.yml` to your repo
2. Configure checkers in `.vigil.config.js`
3. Commit and push
4. Vigil runs on every PR

```json
{
  "security": {
    "enabled": true,
    "rules": ["no-hardcoded-secrets", "no-eval", "no-sql-injection"]
  },
  "types": {
    "enabled": true,
    "strict": true
  },
  "lint": {
    "enabled": true,
    "autoFix": true
  },
  "test": {
    "enabled": true,
    "minCoverage": 80
  }
}
```

## Benefits

✅ Ship AI-generated code with confidence
✅ Catch issues before code review
✅ Educate AI on your standards
✅ Reduce security debt
✅ Maintain code quality at scale

author: Austin H.
title: Monorepo Strategy: When to Use It and How to Scale
content:
# Monorepo Strategy: When to Use It and How to Scale

## Monorepo vs. Polyrepo

### Monorepo (Single Repository)

```
my-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── web/          (Next.js frontend)
│   ├── admin/        (Admin dashboard)
│   └── api/          (Express backend)
├── packages/
│   ├── ui/           (Shared components)
│   ├── utils/        (Shared utilities)
│   ├── types/        (Shared TypeScript types)
│   └── database/     (Database client)
└── tools/
    ├── scripts/      (Build & deploy scripts)
    └── ci/           (CI/CD configs)
```

**Pros:**
- ✅ Shared code without npm publishing
- ✅ Atomic commits across packages
- ✅ Easier refactoring across teams
- ✅ Unified tooling and CI/CD

**Cons:**
- ❌ Larger clones and installs
- ❌ Complex build graphs
- ❌ All teams see all changes
- ❌ Harder to isolate failures

### Polyrepo (Multiple Repositories)

```
my-platform-web/
my-platform-api/
my-platform-admin/
my-platform-ui/
my-platform-types/
my-platform-utils/
```

**Pros:**
- ✅ Fast clones and installs
- ✅ Team isolation and autonomy
- ✅ Independent version control
- ✅ Simpler CI/CD per repo

**Cons:**
- ❌ Shared code requires npm publishing
- ❌ Version coordination overhead
- ❌ Harder cross-package refactoring
- ❌ Duplicate tooling

## When to Use Monorepos

### ✅ Good Fit

1. **Micro-frontends** — Multiple UIs sharing design system
2. **Full-stack apps** — Frontend + backend + shared types
3. **SDKs** — Core lib + language-specific wrappers
4. **Tool suites** — CLI, library, plugins all working together
5. **Startups** — Move fast with shared code

### ❌ Poor Fit

1. **Independent products** — Different teams, schedules
2. **Library ecosystem** — Each lib versioned independently
3. **Open source** — External contributors per package
4. **Large orgs** — Too many teams, too many conflicts

## Setting Up a Monorepo with Nx

### 1. Create Workspace

```bash
npx create-nx-workspace@latest my-platform
cd my-platform
```

### 2. Create Apps and Libraries

```bash
nx generate @nx/next:app web
nx generate @nx/express:app api
nx generate @nx/react:library ui --directory=packages
nx generate @nx/node:library utils --directory=packages
```

### 3. Structure

```
my-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── web/         (Next.js)
│   └── api/         (Express)
├── packages/
│   ├── ui/          (React components)
│   ├── utils/       (Shared functions)
│   └── types/       (TypeScript interfaces)
└── nx.json
```

### 4. Shared Types

```typescript
// packages/types/src/index.ts
export interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'user';
}

export interface CreateUserRequest {
  email: string;
  password: string;
}
```

```typescript
// apps/api/src/routes/users.ts
import { User, CreateUserRequest } from '@my-platform/types';

app.post('/users', (req: CreateUserRequest, res) => {
  const user: User = { id: '1', email: req.email, role: 'user' };
  res.json(user);
});
```

```typescript
// apps/web/src/services/api.ts
import type { User } from '@my-platform/types';

export async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  return fetch(`/api/users/${id}`).then(r => r.json());
}
```

## Build Optimization

### Only Build What Changed

```bash
# Detect dependencies
nx dep-graph

# Build only affected
nx run-many --target=build --projects=tag:scope:web,tag:scope:api

# Run tests on changed packages
nx affected --targets=test
```

## Example: nitsuah Platform

The nitsuah portfolio uses Nx for:

```
apps/
├── nitsuah-io/      (Main portfolio site)
└── admin/           (Content management)

packages/
├── ui/              (Design components)
├── utils/           (Shared functions)
├── types/           (TypeScript interfaces)
└── database/        (Prisma schema & client)
```

One repo, multiple apps, zero code duplication.

## Migration Path

**Start polyrepo → Move to monorepo when:**

1. Teams need to share code frequently
2. Updating shared code requires coordination
3. You're publishing internal packages to npm
4. Build and release processes overlap

**Don't force a monorepo if:**

1. Teams are independent
2. Deployment schedules differ
3. You have external contributors

## Conclusion

Monorepos scale when teams share code and move together. Use Nx or Turbo to manage complexity, and enforce clear boundaries between apps and packages.

excerpt: A practical migration guide from Next.js 14 and React 18 to Next.js 16 and React 19, including the key breaking changes and fixes.
author: Austin H.
title: Upgrading to Next.js 16 and React 19: A Complete Migration Guide
content:
# Upgrading to Next.js 16 and React 19: A Complete Migration Guide ## Overview Next.js 16 and React 19 bring significant improvements. This guide covers key changes, breaking updates, and migration steps. ## Breaking Changes ### 1. React 19 Server Components Server Components are now default. Client components need explicit marking: ```typescript 'use client'; export default function MyComponent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ; } ``` ### 2. Next.js 16 App Router The `pages/` directory is deprecated. Use `app/` instead: ``` app/ ├── layout.tsx ├── page.tsx └── api/ └── route.ts ``` ### 3. Async Server Components Server components can now be async: ```typescript export default async function Page() { const data = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data'); return
{data}
; } ``` ## Migration Steps ### Step 1: Update Dependencies ```bash npm install next@16 react@19 react-dom@19 ``` ### Step 2: Create `app/` Directory ```bash mkdir -p app touch app/layout.tsx app/page.tsx ``` ### Step 3: Convert Pages ```typescript // Before: pages/index.tsx export default function Home() { ... } // After: app/page.tsx export default function Page() { ... } ``` ### Step 4: Update API Routes ```typescript // Before: pages/api/users.ts export default function handler(req, res) { ... } // After: app/api/users/route.ts export async function GET(request: Request) { ... } ``` ## Common Issues ### Hydration Mismatch Server and client render differently. Use `useEffect` for client-only logic: ```typescript const [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false); useEffect(() => { setMounted(true); }, []); if (!mounted) return null; ``` ### Image Optimization Next 16 requires explicit dimensions: ```typescript ``` ### Font Loading Use the new Font API: ```typescript import { Inter } from 'next/font/google'; const inter = Inter({ subsets: ['latin'] }); ``` ## Performance Gains - **Turbopack** — Faster builds - **Tree-shaking** — Smaller bundles - **Image optimization** — Better performance - **Streaming** — Faster page loads with Suspense ## Deployment Deploy to Vercel or self-hosted: ```bash npm run build npm start ``` ## Timeline - **Phase 1**: Update deps and fix types (1-2 days) - **Phase 2**: Migrate pages to `app/` (1 week) - **Phase 3**: Fix hydration issues (3-5 days) - **Phase 4**: Optimize features (ongoing) ## Resources - [Next.js Upgrade Docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/upgrading) - [React 19 Release Notes](https://react.dev/blog/2024/12/05/react-19) - [App Router Guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app) Take your time. Test thoroughly. The improvements are worth it.
